verdict.summary: Arista is the batch's cleanest networking compounder, but the valuation assumes that Ethernet wins a large share of AI back-end and scale-up fabrics. Q2 2026 revenue reached $3.036 billion, up 37.7% year over year; GAAP operating margin was 45.4%, GAAP diluted EPS $0.95 and non-GAAP EPS $1.02. Management guided Q3 revenue to about $3.3 billion and non-GAAP operating margin to 48%-49%. The AI transmission is direct but specific: more accelerators require more high-radix switching, optics, routing and EOS software to keep clusters utilized. Arista's 1.6 Tbps platforms and 100 Tbps system bandwidth target that bottleneck. The balance sheet is exceptional at $13.34 billion cash and no debt, while trailing net margin is 38.4%. The problem is price: 51.1x EV/EBITDA and 22.5x EV/revenue leave little tolerance for customer concentration, merchant-silicon supply or a networking architecture shift. The 76/100 grade measures business quality; the current $200/$187.0299/$211.4499/$214.8899 plan is rejected at only 0.88R/1.15R. Rejected: the preserved structure returns only 0.88R to TP1 and 1.15R to TP2, and the $200 entry is absent from the frozen bars; no activation, order or sizing is allowed.

business.overview:
Arista sells high-speed Ethernet switches, routers, campus products and EOS-based software and services to cloud, AI, data-center and enterprise customers. Product platforms drive most revenue, while software and support deepen lifetime economics.

The AI channel is network utilization: accelerator clusters need scale-up, scale-out and scale-across fabrics with high bandwidth, low latency and telemetry. Arista's 1.6 Tbps Etherlink platforms and EOS automation target the switching layer that determines whether expensive compute sits idle.

The model breaks if hyperscalers moderate capex, adopt proprietary or competing fabrics, or consolidate spending with other vendors. Customer concentration, dependence on merchant silicon and contract manufacturers, and component constraints can disrupt even a strong secular demand cycle. Software support renewals and EOS subscriptions improve visibility, but hardware still depends on cloud deployment cadence and merchant-silicon availability. The model breaks if Microsoft or Meta slows clusters, custom silicon reduces switching intensity, or campus growth cannot offset a pause in AI back-end networks.
business.moat: Arista's moat is EOS: one software image and operating model across a broad switching portfolio, reinforced by cloud-scale telemetry, automation and customer operating familiarity. Hardware can be replicated more readily than a proven network operating environment, but merchant-silicon dependence means the moat is software/architecture-led rather than full-stack silicon control.
